description: The Hotshots is a team of four tackling Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. We're building an Oklahoma fire map and burn calendar that merges 20+ years of NASA satellite fire data into one consistent record, separates wildfires from prescribed burns, and flags unusual fire activity. We love Earth science, data and storytelling. Our team is complete, but we'd welcome mentors with GIS or fire science experience!
summary: HOTSHOTS Fire Calendar is a web app that converts NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots into a single burning activity calendar for the United States. MODIS and VIIRS count fires differently; MODIS counts 86% fewer hotspots than VIIRS. This means that fire activity seems to "jump" when the sensor changes. We have developed a harmonization method to calibrate MODIS to VIIRS on the same time basis, with a separate exchange rate for each of the 11 NOAA climate regions and 12 months and automatic detection and filling in of any gaps in the satellite record. We tested it by rebuilding each year with only MODIS data and found it was accurate to about ±4% each year (monthly R-squared equals 0.98), compared to ±8% and ±86% for no harmonization at all. Click on a state, draw an area, or enter coordinates. You also can choose any date. Near-real-time data lets you see immediately what area burned, which years were the worst, and how this week compares to the same dates in past years. All hotspots can be downloaded as a CSV file or as a one-page summary in PDF. MODIS is no longer in use, but its fire history remains useful for early detection of unusual fire activity at fire spots by responders.
details:
What it does

HOTSHOTS Fire Calendar answers three questions about any part of the United States. When will this area burn? What were the worst years? Is this a comparatively typical week? It combines data from NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections with the most recent seven days of FIRMS near-real-time data into one harmonized record so that the sensor of origin doesn’t matter.

How it works

  1. Data preparation (Python): FIRMS hotspots are carefully selected by looking at their vegetation fires only. We removed low-confidence detections and known static heat sources such as gas flares. They are then assigned to a 0.5° grid, US states, and NOAA climate regions and counted by month.
  2.  Harmonization: MODIS is calibrated to VIIRS using observations taken at the same times of day. Exchange rates are designed for each of 11 NOAA climate regions and each of the 12 months, and then stabilized toward regional and national rates. This is done because VIIRS detects relatively more small fires in some landscapes and seasons. The app automatically detects months with gaps in the satellite record and fills them from the rest of the harmonized record.
  3. Validation: leave-one-year-out testing hides each year. Rebuilds it from MODIS alone. Results for the United States were a ±4% error (R-squared 0.98) versus a ±8% single national ratio and a ±86% with no harmonization. In Georgia, for example, the comparison was  ±6% and  ±65%. We also tested counting fire grid cells for any detections. It ended up performing worse, with an R-squared value of 0.80, so we noted that and decided to keep the better method.
  4. Our app is an interactive US map where viewers can click states, draw a box, or enter coordinates such as latitude/longitude and radius. You can then enter exact date ranges. For a better view, people who access the site can view a burning activity calendar shown as a grid or a circular "fire clock," colored by amount or by difference from the multi-year average, with accessible color ramps.

Key features:

    •    Live card: hotspots this week vs. the same dates in every year since 2018 (for example, Oklahoma at 2.0× its usual, the highest since 2018).

    •    Anomalies vs. multi-year averages, percentiles, and ranks for every month.

    •    Season-start detector, similar-years finder, trend with significance test, and a 6-week seasonal outlook as a traffic light.

    •    "How unusual" map mode showing where activity is above normal.

    •    Downloads: every hotspot in a search (CSV), monthly series, calendar grid, chart images, and a one-click PDF briefing.

    •    Watch list with alerts, simple/expert modes, and a plain-language fire assistant that answers questions from the app's own data.

Benefits and impact

Emergency managers, firefighters, land managers, and scientists get a consistent fire history and can figure out if it’s typical for a specific area. Since MODIS is retiring, our site keeps its previous record and harmonizes it with data from VIIRS, and the app already accepts older FIRMS years (MODIS from 2000) to extend the calendar back to the early 2000s.

Tools and technologies

We used Python (pandas, NumPy, Shapely) for data processing and validation. Then JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for the site’s front and back end. We also utilized D3.js, TopoJSON, PapaParse, and jsPDF for data analysis. The current limits on our project are US state boundaries from us-atlas. Hosted on Netlify.

Creativity

Instead of only converting MODIS counts, we prove the accuracy of this conversion with a test shown in the app. The site can also notice satellite data gaps and turn 25 years' worth of fire data into a "fire clock," providing a weekly comparison.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific validity (sensor resolution, overpass timing, regional and seasonal differences, data gaps, static heat sources)
  • Accessibility (colorblind-safe palettes, labels on every status, table views)
  • Usability for non-experts (simple mode, plain-language briefing) 
  • The outlook is seasonal history, not a forecast
  • The built-in record currently covers 2018–2025 plus the latest week.
